## Purpose

This procedure describes the operation, image capture, and routine
care of the dissecting (stereo) microscopes and compound light
microscopes used in the EA Program laboratory. Dissecting microscopes
provide low-to-moderate magnification (typically 7--45x) with a wide
working distance and are used for sorting biological specimens, gross
morphology, and sample preparation. Compound microscopes provide
higher magnification (40--1000x) with transmitted illumination and are
used for slide-mounted specimens requiring cellular or subcellular
resolution [@murphy2012].

For the Echo Labs Revolve hybrid microscope (which combines upright
compound and inverted configurations with an iPad display), see
[SOP-L211 Revolve Microscope](SOP-L211-revolve-microscope.qmd). The
Revolve has specialized procedures that differ from the conventional
microscopes described here.


## Scope

- **Applies to:** All conventional dissecting (stereo) microscopes and
  compound light microscopes in the EA Program laboratory, including
  units with and without attached cameras
- **Does not apply to:** The Echo Labs Revolve microscope (see
  [SOP-L211](SOP-L211-revolve-microscope.qmd)); electron microscopy;
  confocal microscopy; fluorescence microscopy on non-Revolve
  instruments
- **Location:** EA Program laboratory, SGM 131/133

## Definitions

- **Brightfield microscopy:** Transmitted-light microscopy in which the specimen is illuminated from below and appears against a bright background; the standard mode for stained biological specimens.
- **Compound microscope:** A microscope with two or more lens systems (objective and eyepiece) that produce a magnified image; used for cells, microorganisms, and fine structural detail at total magnifications of 40x--1,000x.
- **Condenser:** A lens assembly below the stage that focuses and concentrates the illumination light onto the specimen; its numerical aperture and position strongly affect image contrast and resolution.
- **Dissecting microscope (stereo microscope):** A low-magnification (typically 7x--45x) binocular microscope that provides a three-dimensional image of intact specimens; used for macroinvertebrate sorting, plant tissue examination, and dissection.
- **Immersion oil:** A synthetic or natural oil with a refractive index matching glass (~1.515); applied between the 100x objective and the coverslip to eliminate the air-glass interface and maximize numerical aperture.
- **Iris diaphragm (condenser diaphragm):** An adjustable aperture in the condenser that controls the cone of illumination; reducing the diaphragm increases contrast but reduces resolution.
- **Parfocal:** The property of a set of objectives that allows switching between magnifications with only minor focus adjustment; standard on modern compound microscopes.
- **Working distance:** The distance between the front lens of the objective and the specimen surface when in focus; decreases with increasing magnification; limits the thickness of specimens that can be accommodated.

## Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Optical:** Prolonged viewing through the eyepieces can cause eye
  strain. Take breaks during extended sorting or identification
  sessions. Adjust the diopter rings to match your vision before
  starting work.
- **Electrical:** Keep liquids away from the illumination base and
  power supply. If liquid enters the base, disconnect power immediately
  and notify the lab manager.
- **Physical:** Compound microscope objectives (especially 40x and
  100x) can contact and crack the slide or cover slip if the stage is
  raised too quickly. Always use the coarse focus knob with caution
  when changing objectives.
- **Chemical/Biological:** Specimens may be preserved in ethanol,
  formalin, or other fixatives. Wear appropriate PPE and handle
  preserved material in a well-ventilated area.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Safety glasses (when not viewing through eyepieces)
- [ ] Lab coat
- [ ] Nitrile gloves (when handling preserved specimens, stains, or
  immersion oil)

### Emergency Procedures

For chemical spills (e.g., ethanol, formalin) on or near a microscope,
clean the spill per
[SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety](SOP-L002-laboratory-safety.qmd) and
[SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling](SOP-L003-hazardous-materials-handling.qmd).
If liquid enters the microscope body, unplug power and contact the lab
manager before attempting further use.

## Procedure

### Choosing the Right Microscope

| Task                                        | Microscope Type  | Typical Magnification |
|:--------------------------------------------|:-----------------|:----------------------|
| Sorting macroinvertebrates from debris       | Dissecting       | 7--20x               |
| Gross specimen identification               | Dissecting       | 10--45x              |
| Examining head capsules, chaetae, gill structures | Compound    | 100--400x            |
| Counting algae or diatoms                   | Compound         | 200--400x            |
| Identifying microplastics on filters        | Dissecting       | 10--45x              |
| Viewing stained tissue sections             | Compound         | 40--1000x            |

### Dissecting Microscope: Setup and Use

1. Plug in the microscope and turn on the illumination using the
   switch on the base. Most units have both **incident** (top) and
   **transmitted** (bottom) light sources. Select the mode appropriate
   for the specimen:
   - Incident light: opaque specimens (insects, soil, rocks)
   - Transmitted light: translucent specimens (small organisms in
     water, thin sections)
   - Both: general sorting when mixed materials are present
2. Adjust the zoom to the lowest magnification (widest field of view)
   to locate the area of interest
3. Place the specimen on the stage plate. Use a white plate for dark
   specimens and a black plate for light or translucent specimens to
   improve contrast.
4. Adjust the interpupillary distance by sliding the eyepiece tubes
   until you see a single merged circle of light
5. Focus using the focus knob (single knob on most stereo scopes).
   With both eyes open, adjust the diopter ring on one eyepiece until
   the image is sharp in both eyes simultaneously.
6. Increase magnification by turning the zoom dial. Refine focus as
   needed.
7. When finished, return the zoom to the lowest setting, remove the
   specimen, turn off the illumination, and unplug the unit if lab
   policy requires it

### Compound Microscope: Setup and Use

1. Plug in the microscope and turn on the light source using the power
   switch. Adjust the intensity to a comfortable level.
2. Rotate the nosepiece to the lowest-magnification objective (4x)
3. Place the prepared slide on the stage, securing it with the stage
   clips. Center the specimen over the condenser aperture.
4. Using the **coarse focus knob**, raise the stage until the specimen
   comes into approximate focus. Watch from the side to avoid driving
   the slide into the objective.
5. Sharpen the image with the **fine focus knob**
6. Adjust the condenser height and the iris diaphragm to optimize
   contrast and resolution. For most work, the condenser should be
   nearly fully raised (close to the slide) and the diaphragm
   partially closed to improve contrast without sacrificing too much
   resolution [@murphy2012].
7. Increase magnification by rotating the nosepiece to the next
   objective (10x, then 40x). Refocus with the fine focus knob only.

::: {.callout-important}
### Avoid Slide Damage
When switching from the 10x to the 40x objective, watch from the side
to confirm that the longer 40x lens does not contact the cover slip.
If the working distance is too short, lower the stage slightly before
rotating the objective into position.
:::

### Using Oil Immersion (100x Objective)

1. Focus the specimen at 40x first
2. Rotate the nosepiece to an empty position (no objective in the
   light path)
3. Place a single small drop of immersion oil directly on the cover
   slip at the point of illumination. Do not use excess oil.
4. Rotate the 100x objective into position. The front element of the
   lens should contact the oil without trapping an air bubble.
5. Focus carefully using the **fine focus knob only**
6. After use, immediately clean the 100x objective with lens cleaning
   solution and lint-free tissue. Wipe gently from center to edge.
   Never allow oil to dry on the lens.
7. Clean the slide or dispose of it as appropriate

### Capturing Images (Camera-Equipped Units)

1. Focus the specimen and center the region of interest in the field
   of view
2. Open the camera software on the connected computer (software varies
   by camera model; consult the lab manager for the current setup)
3. Adjust exposure and white balance in the software to match the
   illumination
4. Capture the image. Record the magnification, scale bar, and sample
   ID in the file name or metadata.
5. Use a consistent file-naming convention:
   `YYYY-MM-DD_SampleID_Magnification_Mode.jpg`
6. Export images to the project data folder

### Shutdown and Daily Maintenance

1. Remove the specimen from the stage
2. Rotate the nosepiece to the lowest-magnification objective (4x on
   compound; lowest zoom on dissecting)
3. If oil immersion was used, clean the 100x objective immediately
   (see Section 6.4, step 6)
4. Wipe any residue from the stage with a lint-free tissue
5. Turn off the light source and unplug if required by lab policy
6. Cover the microscope with a dust cover


## Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

### Optics Cleaning

If specks or smudges appear in the field of view that do not move when
the specimen is translated, the optics need cleaning:

1. Start with a few short bursts of compressed gas duster to remove
   loose dust from the objectives and oculars. Do not invert the can.
2. For objective lens surfaces, apply a small amount of lens cleaning
   solution to a piece of lint-free optical tissue and gently wipe in
   a circular motion from center to edge. Do not use dry tissue on
   coated optics.
3. Clean the oculars (eyepieces) the same way. Fingerprints on the
   eye lens are the most common source of image degradation.
4. For persistent contamination on internal optics, contact the lab
   manager. Do not disassemble the microscope.

### Illumination Check

- Replace burned-out bulbs promptly. LED-equipped units should not
  require bulb replacement during normal use.
- If transmitted light appears uneven, check that the condenser is
  properly centered and the iris diaphragm is functioning.

### Image Quality Checklist

Before accepting a micrograph for publication or analysis, verify:

- Focus is sharp across the region of interest
- Illumination is even (no hot spots or vignetting)
- A scale bar or magnification is recorded
- The specimen is oriented consistently with project conventions


## Waste Disposal

| Waste Type                            | Disposal Method                      |
|:--------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|
| Used immersion oil tissues            | Standard trash                       |
| Used microscope slides (non-hazardous) | Broken-glass box if glass           |
| Biological specimen waste             | Biohazard bag if applicable; autoclave before disposal per [SOP-L112](SOP-L112-autoclave-sterilization.qmd) |
| Preserved specimen waste (ethanol)    | Flammable waste container            |
| Preserved specimen waste (formalin)   | Hazardous waste; dispose through EH&S |
| Spent lens cleaning solution          | Standard trash (small volumes on tissues) |

## Training Record

Before using dissecting or compound microscopes independently,
personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Complete [SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety](SOP-L002-laboratory-safety.qmd)
   training
3. Demonstrate proper setup, focusing, magnification changes, and
   shutdown of both dissecting and compound microscopes under
   supervision
4. If oil immersion work is required, demonstrate proper oil
   application, focusing, and cleanup
5. If image capture is required, demonstrate camera operation and
   correct file naming
6. Be signed off by the PI or lab manager


## Appendix A: Microscope Anatomy Quick Reference {.appendix}

### Dissecting (Stereo) Microscope

| Component                | Function                                    |
|:-------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| Eyepieces (oculars)      | Binocular viewing; 10x magnification (typical) |
| Zoom dial                | Continuously adjustable magnification (e.g., 0.7--4.5x objective) |
| Focus knob               | Single knob for coarse/fine focus           |
| Stage plate              | Removable; white and black plates for contrast |
| Incident light           | Top illumination for opaque specimens       |
| Transmitted light        | Bottom illumination for translucent specimens |
| Diopter adjustment       | On one or both eyepieces; corrects for vision differences between eyes |

### Compound Microscope

| Component                | Function                                    |
|:-------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| Eyepieces (oculars)      | Binocular viewing; 10x magnification (typical) |
| Nosepiece (turret)       | Holds and rotates objective lenses          |
| Objective lenses         | 4x, 10x, 40x, 100x (oil); determine magnification |
| Stage                    | Holds slide; translatable via X/Y controls  |
| Condenser                | Focuses transmitted light onto the specimen |
| Iris diaphragm           | Controls cone angle of illumination; affects contrast and resolution |
| Coarse focus knob        | Rapid focus (large movements)               |
| Fine focus knob          | Precise focus (small movements)             |
| Light intensity control  | Adjusts brightness of the transmitted light source |


## Appendix B: Total Magnification Reference {.appendix}

Total magnification = eyepiece magnification $\times$ objective
magnification. For standard 10x eyepieces:

| Objective | Total Magnification | Typical Use                        |
|:----------|:--------------------|:-----------------------------------|
| 4x        | 40x                 | Scanning; locating regions of interest |
| 10x       | 100x                | General observation                |
| 40x       | 400x                | Detailed cellular structure        |
| 100x (oil) | 1000x              | Fine detail; bacteria, diatom striae, chromosomes |
